metadata.note: Myrtle Beach's rail history: a brand-new short line reaching a brand-new resort town, riding in on the back of an older lumber railroad that already connected to the wider Atlantic Coast Line network. The Conway Seashore Railroad (chartered 1899, opened 1900) built southeast from Conway, SC to the developing settlement then called 'New Town' -- present-day Myrtle Beach -- as both a freight and passenger line. It connected at Conway to the older Wilmington, Chadbourn and Conway Railroad (built by the Chadbourn Lumber Company to haul timber, exact construction year not sourced but operating by the mid-1890s), which ran north to a junction with the ACL's own Wilmington-Pee Dee main line at Chadbourn, NC -- giving Myrtle Beach a real connection to the national network from day one. Both lines ended up under Atlantic Coast Line ownership: the Chadbourn-Conway line by 1898, the renamed Conway Coast and Western (as of 1904) by 1911-12, after which both were operated together as the ACL's Myrtle Beach Branch. ACL opened a substantial new Myrtle Beach station in 1937, heavily used by tourists and, during and after WWII, military personnel from the nearby air base. Regular passenger service ended Mar 16 1955; a reduced mixed freight/passenger train continued to run Myrtle Beach-Chadbourn for a time afterward. The last documented passenger movement of any kind was a one-off special: an Oct 23 1986 charter from Myrtle Beach to Conway for a Democratic Party rally, decades after regular service had ended. GEOMETRY METHODOLOGY: real-traced through OpenStreetMap active/abandoned-rail data (Overpass API, shortest-path graph search) -- traced lengths (25.7 km / 16.0 mi Conway-Myrtle Beach, 62.4 km / 38.8 mi Conway-Chadbourn) match the short local distances involved.
